lesson.text: Quick memory: in grade 4 you met solids, liquids and gases. Which one takes the shape of its container and has a flat top? A liquid.
Everything around you is matter: anything that takes up space and has mass. Water, air, rock and even you are made of matter.
All matter is made of particles far too small to see, even with a magnifying glass.
Air is matter too. You can't see air, but you can feel it push when the wind blows. And you can watch a balloon grow as air fills it.
When sugar dissolves in water, it seems to vanish. But the tiny sugar particles are still there, spread through the water.
In a solid the particles are packed tightly and stay in place. In a liquid they slide past each other. In a gas they spread far apart and zoom around.
Try it in the world: at a Science Lab bench, do "Melting and freezing": the same particles go from solid to liquid and back. Next: mass is kept when things change.

exercises.prompt: What is all matter made of?
exercises.hint: Think smaller than a grain of sand.
choices: tiny particles too small to see
exercises.explain: All matter is made of particles far too small to see.

exercises.prompt: Air is matter.
exercises.hint: Does air take up space?
exercises.explain: Yes: air takes up space and has mass, so it is matter.

exercises.prompt: In which state are the particles packed tightly together?
exercises.hint: Think of an ice cube.
exercises.explain: In a solid, the particles are packed tightly and stay in place.

exercises.prompt: Which one is matter?
exercises.hint: Which one takes up space?
exercises.explain: The air in a balloon takes up space and has mass. Shadows and rainbows are light, not matter.

exercises.prompt: You can see a single particle of sugar with your eyes.
exercises.hint: How small are particles?
exercises.explain: No: particles are far too small to see. A sugar grain has billions of them.

exercises.prompt: Sugar is stirred into water and disappears. What happened to it?
exercises.hint: Can you still taste it?
choices: Its particles spread through the water.
exercises.explain: The sugar particles are still there, spread out too thinly to see.

exercises.prompt: How can you show that air takes up space?
exercises.hint: What fills a balloon?
choices: Blow up a balloon and watch it grow.
exercises.explain: The balloon grows because air takes up space inside it.

exercises.prompt: Which state of matter spreads out to fill any container?
exercises.hint: Think of a smell filling a room.
exercises.explain: A gas's particles spread out to fill the whole container.

exercises.prompt: You can smell soup from across the room because tiny particles travel through the air.
exercises.hint: How does a smell reach you?
exercises.explain: Yes: tiny particles from the soup spread through the air to your nose.

exercises.prompt: Order from particles packed most tightly to most spread out.
exercises.hint: Solid, liquid, gas.
exercises.explain: Ice (solid), water (liquid), steam (gas).

exercises.prompt: Salty water is left in the sun. The water dries up and salt crystals appear. What does this show?
exercises.hint: Where could the salt come from?
choices: The salt was in the water all along.
exercises.explain: The salt particles were spread through the water the whole time.

exercises.prompt: A pump pushes more air into a bike tyre, and the tyre gets harder. Why?
exercises.hint: What did the pump add?
choices: More air particles are packed inside.
exercises.explain: More particles of air are squeezed inside, pushing on the tyre.

exercises.prompt: Why can you walk through air but not through a wall?
exercises.hint: Compare a gas with a solid.
choices: Air's particles are far apart; a wall's aren't.
exercises.explain: A gas's particles are far apart and move; a solid's are packed tightly.

exercises.prompt: When a puddle dries up, its water particles are destroyed.
exercises.hint: Where does the water go?
exercises.explain: No: the water particles go into the air as water vapour.

exercises.prompt: Which model best shows a gas?
exercises.hint: Gas particles spread out.
choices: a few dots far apart, moving fast
exercises.explain: A gas's particles are far apart and move quickly.

exercises.prompt: Sort the things: matter or not matter?
exercises.hint: Does it take up space and have mass?
exercises.explain: Air, water, rock and steam take up space and have mass: matter. A shadow and a rainbow are light, not matter.

exercises.prompt: Match each state to how its particles behave.
exercises.hint: Think of an ice cube, a glass of water and steam.
exercises.explain: Solid: packed tightly, in place. Liquid: close, sliding past each other. Gas: spread far apart, zooming around.

exercises.prompt: Solid, liquid or gas?
exercises.hint: Does it keep its shape, pour, or spread out to fill the air?
exercises.explain: Ice and a rock are solids, water is a liquid, and steam is a gas.

exercises.prompt: Sort the descriptions by state of matter.
exercises.hint: Think of ice, water and steam.
exercises.explain: Solid: packed tightly in place, so it keeps its shape. Liquid: the particles slide past each other, so it takes its container's shape. Gas: far apart and zooming, so it fills the whole container.

exercises.prompt: Match each everyday clue to what it shows about particles.
items: you smell soup across a room
a balloon grows as you blow
exercises.hint: Each clue shows particles doing something too small to see.
exercises.explain: Smelling soup: its particles travel through the air. A growing balloon: air takes up space. Vanishing sugar: its particles spread out, too small to see. A harder tyre: more air particles packed inside.
